structured_data.name: Abalone
structured_data.description: Play Abalone against a bot at eight strengths, pass and play on one device, or invite someone to a game online. Nine board setups and a full move history. Free in the browser.
structured_data.audience: Board game players and strategy game enthusiasts

offline.heading: Play Abalone vs the computer or a friend
offline.intro: Play Abalone against the computer or with a friend on the same device, free in your browser. Pick one of eight bots, from Gus (level 1) to Magnus (level 8), or choose Pass & Play and hand the screen back and forth. No download, no account.

strength.title: How strong is the computer?
strength.intro: The eight bots are one player at different strengths, not one good player made to blunder.
strength.low: Levels 1 to 4 (Gus, Milo, Nora, Theo) look one move ahead and have habits you can use. Gus and Milo chase your marbles, push forward without a plan and sometimes sit near the rim. Gus also plays a random move about 1 time in 7. The habits fade level by level, and none of the four ever plans a push.
strength.middle: Levels 5 and 6 (Iris, Victor) still look one move ahead but start lining up pushes and crowding marbles near the edge. Victor cares much more about the center.
strength.high: Levels 7 and 8 (Clara, Magnus) play like Victor but look two and three moves ahead, so they see your reply coming.

beat.title: How to beat the Abalone computer

tips.center: Take the center first. Every bot values the middle. Hold it and you hold the pushes.
tips.touching: Keep your marbles touching. Against the low levels, a lone marble is the one thing they can reach. Do not leave one.
tips.rim: Do not trust the rim. Bots from level 5 up look for marbles near the edge. Keep yours one row in.
tips.overextend: Wait for the weak bots to overextend. Levels 1 and 2 charge forward. Let them arrive broken up, then push.
tips.ahead: Against levels 7 and 8, think two moves ahead. They see your reply, so set up a push they cannot stop with a single move.
tips.learn: Use Hint and Undo to learn. Both are in the game, and the eval bar shows who is ahead.

beat.more: The plan behind these is in the <strategy>strategy tips</strategy> and the <openings>opening moves</openings>.

local.title: Two players on one device (Pass & Play)
local.body: Choose Pass & Play, set up the board and take turns on the same screen. Black moves first. Same rules as against the computer, and Undo works too. Hint and the eval bar are only in games against the computer. To play across two devices, <online>play online</online>.

free.question: Can I play Abalone against the computer for free?
free.answer: Yes. Choose vs Computer, pick one of eight bots and start. It runs in your browser with no download and no account.

beat.question: How do I beat the Abalone AI?
beat.answer: Hold the center, keep your marbles in touching groups and stay off the edge row. Weak bots chase and overextend. Strong ones look several moves ahead, so build a push they cannot stop with a single move.

levels.question: How many difficulty levels does the computer have?
levels.answer: Eight, from Gus at level 1 to Magnus at level 8. The first four have habits you can use against them. Levels 1 to 6 look one move ahead, Clara two and Magnus three.

same_device.question: Can two people play Abalone on the same device?
same_device.answer: Yes. Choose Pass & Play and take turns on one screen. Black moves first.

random.question: Does the computer ever play randomly?
random.answer: The weaker bots sometimes do. Gus ignores its own search about 15% of the time, Milo 10%, Nora 8% and Theo 5%. From level 5 up the bot always plays its best move.

offline.question: Can I play without an internet connection?
offline.answer: Yes, once the page has loaded. The computer runs on your device, so a game against it or a Pass & Play game keeps going with no connection. Only online games and your account need the internet.

rules.title: How to play
rules.heading: Abalone rules: how to play
rules.intro: You play Abalone by taking turns to move up to three marbles one space. A bigger group can push a smaller one. Push six of your opponent's marbles off the board to win. When you are ready, <online>play Abalone online</online> or <offline>try it against the computer</offline>.

goal.title: The goal
goal.body: Push six of your opponent's marbles off the edge of the board. The first player to do it wins. You cannot win by trapping marbles, only by pushing them out.

turns.title: Who moves first
turns.body: Players take turns, one move each. Black goes first. On your turn you must move; you cannot pass.

directions.title: How marbles move
directions.body: A marble moves one space to any of the six neighbouring spaces. The board is a hexagon, so each space touches six others. There are no jumps and no captures by jumping.
directions.caption: The six directions.

move.title: Moving one, two or three marbles
move.body: You may move one, two or three of your own marbles in one turn. Two or three marbles must touch in a straight line, and they move together one space. There are two kinds of move:
move.inline: In-line move: the group moves along the line it points, like a train. The front marble steps into the next space.
move.broadside: Side step (broadside): the group moves sideways, each marble into the empty space next to it. All the target spaces must be empty.
move.limit: You can never move more than three marbles, and never marbles that are not in a straight line.
move.inline_caption: In line: the row advances the way it points.
move.broadside_caption: Broadside: the row steps sideways onto empty spaces.

push.title: Pushing: the sumito
push.body: A push is called a sumito. It is an in-line move into a space held by your opponent. You need more marbles in the line than your opponent:
push.conditions: Two more conditions: the space behind the pushed marbles must be empty (or off the board), and the push must be in line, never a side step. Equal numbers never push, so 2 against 2 and 3 against 3 are a standoff. You can never push your own marbles.
push.ok_caption: Three against two: the line shifts one space.
push.blocked_caption: Equal numbers never move, and you never push your own.

capture.title: Pushing marbles off the board
capture.body: If a push moves an opposing marble past the edge, it is out of the game. That is one point toward your six. A marble next to the edge is in danger: if you are pushed there with fewer marbles than your opponent has in line, you lose it.
capture.caption: Two against one at the edge: black is out.

win.title: How to win
win.body: The first player to push six marbles off wins. If you cannot stop a push, break the line: move a marble next to the attacker so it is outnumbered, or pull back from the edge.

setups.title: Starting positions
setups.body: Every layout starts with 14 marbles each.
setups.standard: <name>Standard:</name> each side starts on its two nearest rows (black at the bottom, white at the top), with three marbles in the middle of the third row. The armies face each other and no pushing is possible on move one. Best for learning.
setups.belgian_daisy: <name>Belgian daisy:</name> marbles start in four flower-shaped clusters, one in each corner. Black and white alternate around the board (white top-left and bottom-right, black top-right and bottom-left). The armies touch on the first move, so play is fast and tactical. Popular in tournaments because it is fairer than the standard layout.
setups.german_daisy: <name>German daisy:</name> four flower-shaped clusters again, with the same colours as the Belgian daisy (white upper left and lower right, black upper right and lower left), but set in from the corners toward the sides. The clusters start further apart, so the opening is more open.
setups.others: Others in the game: Dutch daisy, Swiss daisy, Alien, Domination, Infiltration and The Wall. Choose one when you start a game.
setups.openings: Want a safe start? See our <openings>Abalone opening moves for beginners</openings>.
setups.compare: Compare them in detail: <positions>Abalone starting positions</positions>.

faq.title: Frequently asked

first.question: Who goes first in Abalone?
first.answer: Black goes first, then players take turns. You cannot pass.

diagonal.question: Can I move marbles diagonally?
diagonal.answer: Every direction on the hexagon grid counts as one of six directions; there is no other kind of diagonal.

single.question: Can a single marble push?
single.answer: No. A push needs at least two marbles against one.

own_push.question: Can you push your own marbles?
own_push.answer: No. A push only moves your opponent's marbles. If your own marble is in the way, the move is not legal.

draw.question: Can Abalone end in a draw?
draw.answer: Yes. In this game, if the same position comes up a third time with the same player to move, it is a draw.

faq.strategy_link: Try the strategy tips: <strategy>Abalone strategy: 7 tips</strategy>.

strategy.title: Strategy
strategy.heading: Abalone strategy: 7 tips to win
strategy.intro: To win at Abalone, keep your marbles together near the center and count before every push. Push six of your opponent's marbles off the board. Practise in a <offline>free game against the computer</offline>. New here? Read the <rules>Abalone rules</rules> first.

center.title: 1. Control the center
center.body: Marbles in the middle have six neighbours and room to move. Marbles on the edge are one push from out. Early on, move your outer marbles toward the center and keep the opponent's off it. A player who owns the center decides where the fight happens.

groups_of_three.title: 2. Keep your groups of three
groups_of_three.body: Three connected marbles in a line can push two, and cannot easily be pushed. Move so your marbles stay in compact, touching groups. A lone marble is a target, and a long thin chain is easy to cut.

edge.title: 3. Stay away from the edge
edge.body: Every marble on the outer ring can be lost to a single sumito. Only go there to attack, and only when your push comes first. If your marble is on the edge and your opponent has a line pointing at it, move it or block the line this turn.

count.title: 4. Count before you push
count.body: A push needs more marbles in line than your opponent, and an empty space behind. Before each push, count both lines and check what your move leaves open. A push that breaks up your own group often gives the marble straight back.

opening.title: 5. Choose your opening on purpose
opening.body: In the standard layout, nobody can push on move one, so develop toward the center in small steps and keep your three-marble rows. In a Belgian daisy the armies touch at once: look for the first sumito and defend your weakest cluster. Try each layout against the computer to learn what changes. Need a safe first move? See the Abalone opening moves.

attack_as_a_group.title: 6. Attack as a group, not as a hero
attack_as_a_group.body: Pushing one marble off with a lone stack of three is rare. More often you win by pressuring an edge marble with two groups, so your opponent cannot answer both. Bring a second line to the same area before you commit.

tempo.title: 7. Win the tempo, not the marble
tempo.body: Do not rush for the first point. A player who leads by a marble but has scattered groups often loses the next three exchanges. Make safe moves that leave your opponent with only bad ones; Abalone is a game of who runs out of good moves first.

items.lone_edge: Moving a marble alone to the edge to "threaten" something.
items.split_three: Splitting a three into two twos just before the opponent's three arrives.
items.leave_hole: Pushing when it leaves a hole your opponent steps into.

solved.question: Is Abalone solved?
solved.answer: No. Only very small versions of the board have been solved. The full board of 61 cells has no known perfect strategy, so the tips above still decide most games.

first_move.question: What is the best first move?
first_move.answer: It depends on the layout. See <openings>Abalone opening moves</openings>.

openings.title: Opening moves
openings.heading: Abalone opening moves for beginners
openings.intro: The first few moves of an Abalone game set up the fight that follows. This page covers the <positions>starting position</positions>, which opening moves are safe, and how the daisy layouts change the first turns. Not sure how a push works? Read the <rules>Abalone rules</rules> first, then try these ideas in a <offline>free game against the computer</offline>. Once the opening feels familiar, read the <strategy>Abalone strategy tips</strategy>.

start.title: The starting position
start.body: In the standard layout each player has 14 marbles: their two nearest rows (five and six marbles) plus three in the middle of the third row. Black sits at the bottom, white at the top, and black moves first. The armies face each other across three empty rows, so nobody can push on move one. Compare all three layouts in Abalone starting positions.

safe.title: Safe first moves
safe.body: With no push possible yet, use the opening to build, not to attack. Step a marble or a short row from the front toward the center in small moves, and keep your marbles touching. A group of three in a line can push two and is hard to push, so a tight formation is a good start. Do not send one marble alone ahead of the rest.

sidestep.title: Side steps and in-line moves
sidestep.body: Early on, a side step (a broadside move) lets a row slide sideways while staying together. An in-line move advances the row the way it points. Both are legal on turn one; the difference is what they leave behind. Before you move, check that you are not opening a gap your opponent can use.

daisy.title: Opening on a daisy layout
daisy.body: In the Belgian daisy the armies start in four flower-shaped clusters and touch from the first move, so a sumito can come early. Look for a push you can make, and for the cluster you could lose a marble from. The German daisy has the same four clusters but starts them further apart, which gives you a few quiet moves first. For the full comparison, see Belgian daisy vs German daisy.

others.title: Other starting layouts
others.body: The game also has the Dutch daisy, Swiss daisy, Alien, Domination, Infiltration and The Wall. Each changes which marbles touch at the start. Pick one when you start a game, and play the same layout a few times to learn its first moves.

items.lone_runner: Sending one marble to the middle on its own, where it can be surrounded.
items.rush_edge: Moving toward the edge early, where a single push can knock a marble off.
items.ignore_daisy: Playing a daisy layout like the standard one and missing an early sumito.

positions.title: Starting positions
positions.heading: Abalone starting positions
positions.intro: Abalone has three main starting positions: standard, Belgian daisy and German daisy. Each player gets 14 marbles and black moves first. Standard is best for learning; in the daisies the armies meet sooner. See the <rules>rules</rules> and <opening>opening moves</opening>.

glance.caption: The three main Abalone starting positions compared

standard.title: Standard layout
standard.label: Standard starting position
standard.body: In the standard layout each player has 14 marbles: their two nearest rows (five and six marbles) plus three in the middle of the third row. Black sits at the bottom, white at the top, and black moves first. The armies face each other across three empty rows, so nobody can push on move one.
standard.next: Start here if you are new, then read <opening>opening moves</opening>.

belgian_daisy.title: Belgian daisy
belgian_daisy.label: Belgian daisy starting position
belgian_daisy.body: Marbles start in four flower-shaped clusters, one in each corner. White is top-left and bottom-right, black top-right and bottom-left. The armies touch on the first move, so a sumito can come early: look for a push you can make and for the cluster you could lose a marble from.
belgian_daisy.history: Players moved to daisy starts because the standard layout lets a careful player build a defensive wedge and avoid attacks indefinitely; the Belgian daisy was adopted by top players in 1999 to revitalize the game.

german_daisy.title: German daisy
german_daisy.label: German daisy starting position
german_daisy.body: Four flower-shaped clusters again, same colours as the Belgian daisy, but set in from the corners toward the sides. The clusters start further apart, so you get a few quiet moves to build groups of three before the first contact.

compare.title: Belgian daisy vs German daisy
compare.body: Both use four clusters and the same colours. The difference is distance: in the Belgian daisy the armies touch from move one; in the German daisy they start further apart. Pick the Belgian daisy for sharp early fights and the German daisy if you want time to set up first. Not sure? Play both against the computer.

others.title: Other layouts
others.body: Dutch daisy, Swiss daisy, Alien, Domination, Infiltration and The Wall are also in the game. Choose one when you start a game.

marbles.question: How many marbles does each player start with in Abalone?
marbles.answer: Each player starts with 14 marbles, in every layout on this page.

belgian.question: What is the Belgian daisy in Abalone?
belgian.answer: A starting position with four flower-shaped clusters, one in each corner. The armies touch from the first move.

difference.question: What is the difference between the Belgian daisy and the German daisy?
difference.answer: Both use the same four clusters and colours. The German daisy sets them in from the corners toward the sides, so they start further apart.

beginners.question: Which Abalone starting position is best for beginners?
beginners.answer: The standard layout, because nobody can push on move one.

why_daisy.question: Why do players use the daisy layouts?
why_daisy.answer: They make it less likely that a defensive wedge stalls the game. Top players adopted the Belgian daisy in 1999 to revitalize the game.

try.title: Try them
try.more_reading: Once you have picked a layout, read the <strategy>Abalone strategy tips</strategy>.

playOnline.heading: Play Abalone online with a friend
playOnline.intro: You can play Abalone online with a friend for free, right in your browser. Create a free account, make a private invite link, and send it to whoever you want to play. The game starts when they open the link and accept, and you each take your turn whenever you like.
playOnline.no_account: No account? Play the computer now

steps.title: How to play Abalone with a friend online

items.invite: Choose a board setup and your side, then tap "Invite with a link".
items.accept: Your friend opens it, creates an account or signs in, and taps "Accept and play".

free.question: Is online Abalone free?
free.answer: Yes. Playing online costs nothing. You need a free account.

sign_up.question: Do I need to sign up?
sign_up.answer: Yes, online games need an account, a username and a password. To play without one, <offline>play the computer or pass and play</offline>.

friend.question: How do I play Abalone with a friend?
friend.answer: Make an invite link from the Online page and send it. They accept and the game starts. You can also invite a friend by username.

private.question: Is the invite link private?
private.answer: Only whoever has the link can accept it, and only one person can. It expires after 7 days.

same_time.question: Do we have to be online at the same time?
same_time.answer: No. Take your turns whenever you like.

code.question: Is there a game code?
code.answer: No, you share a link instead.

guide.title: How to move
guide.select_body: Tap one of your marbles. Tap up to two more in a straight line to move them together.
guide.direction_body: Tap a highlighted space to move there. A longer line can push a shorter line of your opponent's.
guide.win_body: Push six of your opponent's marbles off the edge of the board and you win.
